fetched_contents.text: Von Willebrand Disease and Pregnancy: Management Protocol From Labor to the Postpartum Period Abstract Von Willebrand disease (VWD) is a hemostatic disorder characterized by a quantitative or qualitative deficiency of the Von Willebrand factor (VWF). It affects males and females equally. This pathology has more severe clinical manifestations in females of reproductive age, with a mean age of diagnosis at 19 years. In the pregnant patient, Von Willebrand disease poses an increased risk of complications during labor or the postpartum period, attributed to a higher likelihood of experiencing postpartum hemorrhage and its consequential complications arising from transfusion support and multiorgan injury due to tissue hypoperfusion. We present the case of a 25-year-old G3P2V2A1 patient with a preexisting diagnosis of Von Willebrand disease prior to gestation. The institutional protocol for managing this condition involved the administration of Von Willebrand factor and factor VIII (FVIII) during vaginal delivery and the postpartum period. This resulted in the effective control of perinatal and postpartum bleeding, with an elevation in Von Willebrand factor levels, thereby avoiding the need for blood transfusions and signs of secondary hypoperfusion. This case underscores the significance of specialized management for Von Willebrand disease during pregnancy and childbirth, emphasizing adherence to institutional protocols involving specific hemostatic factors. The collaborative efforts of a multidisciplinary team, including hematologists, obstetricians, and other healthcare professionals, are crucial for the comprehensive care of females with this condition during the perinatal period. Keywords: von willebrand disease, coagulation disorders, obstetric hemorrhage, blood pathology, high-risk pregnancy Introduction Von Willebrand disease (VWD) is a clotting disorder characterized by a quantitative or qualitative deficiency of the Von Willebrand factor (VWF) [1]. Synthesized in endothelial cells and megakaryocytes, VWF plays a key role in primary and secondary hemostasis through its interaction with various platelet adhesion and aggregation receptors. It also participates in secondary hemostasis, acting as a factor VIII (FVIII) transporter to avoid the latter’s activated protein C-mediated breakdown in plasma [2,3]. Although the prevalence of all forms of VWD is estimated at 0.6%-1.3%, the symptomatic form of the disease, which requires specific treatment, affects males and females equally [4], with a mean age of 19 years at the time of diagnosis in females [5]. This condition is classified into three types, the most common being type 1 in 70%-78% of cases, characterized by partial quantitative VWF deficiency. Type 2 is characterized by a qualitative VWF deficiency and is subdivided into subtypes: subtype A, subtype B, subtype M, and subtype N, in which VWF has very low factor VIII affinity. Finally, VWD type 3 is characterized by a complete quantitative VWF deficiency [1]. The disease has an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern in types 2N and 3 and a dominant autosomal pattern in types 1, 2A, 2B, and 2M [3,6]. Diagnosis is usually suspected early in life due to manifestations such as gum bleeding, epistaxis, abnormal uterine bleeding, and, in more severe cases, gastrointestinal bleeding. The diagnosis is confirmed by means of VWF quantification based on antigen levels or VWF and clotting factor VII activity. Since a wide heterogeneity of phenotypes and of the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms is associated with this disorder, a prompt and careful evaluation of pregnant women with VWD is requested in order to plan the most appropriate treatment at time of parturition. VWF and FVIII increase significantly during pregnancy in normal women, already within the first trimester, reaching levels by far >100 U/dL by the time of parturition. Women with VWD, levels at baseline of VWF and FVIII >30 U/dL have us a high likelihood to achieve normal levels at the end of pregnancy; thus specific anti-hemorrhagic prophylaxis is seldom required. Women with basal level <20 U/dL usually have a poor increase since most of these women carry mutations associated with increased VWF clearance or are compound heterozygous for different VWF mutations; that prevent the achievement of satisfactory hemostatic levels. While women with mutations associated with increased clearance show a full, albeit transitory correction of their hemostatic deficiency after desmopressin administration, compound heterozygous need replacement therapy because they do not respond well to this agent. Patients with abnormal VWF:RCo/VWF:Ag ratio at baseline (e.g. <0.6), typically associated with type 2 VWD, maintain the abnormality throughout pregnancy and VWF:RCo usually does not attain safe levels ≥50 U/dL. These women require replacement therapy with VWF-FVIII concentrates. Delayed post-partum bleeding may occur when replacement therapy is not continued for some days. Tranexamic acid may be useful at discharge to avoid excessive lochia. Clinical manifestations are mainly represented by mucous membrane and soft tissue bleeding and their severity is variable depending on the degree of VWF and FVIII reduction.2 Women with VWD are at particularly high risk of bleeding because of menorrhagia and delivery. Women may undergo to naturally-occurring physiological events (menstruation, pregnancy and parturition) that may cause undue bleeding complications even in absence of a specific bleeding disorder. At the time of delivery, several obstetric complications may cause bleeding with or without associated hematologic alterations.3 A standard definition of post-partum hemorrhage (PPH) considers the threshold of 500 mL blood loss for vaginal delivery and of 1,000 mL for caesarean section.4 Rates of PPH in Western Countries based on hospital discharge may range from 3 to 6%, while cases needing blood transfusion are as low as 1%.3 Uterine atony is still the leading cause of hemorrhage at parturition accounting for approximately 75% of all cases with PPH and may be burdened with a high risk of being transfused or even death in otherwise healthy women.3,5 Of course, these complications may add to the inherent risk of bleeding in women with inherited bleeding disorder. Risk of bleeding at parturition in women with von Willebrand disease There are conflicting results in the literature about the correct estimation of the risk and the severity of bleeding at parturition in women with VWD. Historical series reported percentages of VWD women with post-partum bleeding ranging from 15 to 60%.6–10 This uncertainty is also reported when women with wide range of basal FVIII and VWF are included among the type 1 patients. fetched_contents.text: Congenital and acquired bleeding disorders in pregnancy Abstract Obstetrical hematology represents challenges not only for the patient, but also for her progeny. In particular, bleeding disorders, both congenital and acquired, not only present problems both for delivery and in the immediate postpartum period, but also may have significant implications for the fetus and neonate. Women with congenital bleeding disorders or who are carriers of X-linked or autosomal disorders should be counseled prior to conception so that pregnancy can be safely undertaken with careful preparation. A treatment plan should be set up by a specialized care team that includes the hematologist, obstetrician, and anesthesiologist; the patient should be followed closely during pregnancy, through delivery, and in the immediate postpartum period. Acquired disorders of hemostasis that occur with pregnancy may present particular diagnostic difficulties and require rapid diagnosis and management. ---------------------------------------- Learning Objectives * List methods of preterm diagnosis of congenital bleeding disorders * Understand management strategies of factor deficiencies in pregnancy * Discuss the differential diagnosis of thrombocytopenia in pregnancy and its management Women with a variety of congenital and acquired bleeding disorders are commonly referred to the hematologist by the obstetrician to help with management of pregnancy, in particular to prepare with delivery. Careful planning and monitoring during gestation is essential in patients with known abnormalities. Acquired abnormalities of hemostasis may present particular difficulties with diagnosis and management. With specialized expert care, the majority of women with these disorders can safely deliver a healthy infant. Congenital disorders of hemostasis Women with inherited bleeding disorders face hemostatic challenges during various stages of pregnancy. Women who are carriers may have abnormally low factor levels and be at risk as well. Bleeding may occur at the time of delivery and postpartum, but the patient may also be at risk following spontaneous pregnancy loss, during diagnostic procedures, and during termination of pregnancy. Women with inherited blood disorders planning a pregnancy should be evaluated by a hematologist and a high-risk obstetrician expert in the management of these disorders. Congenital disorders of hemostasis require consideration not only for the bleeding risks of the mother: the risk of the fetus having inherited the bleeding tendency must also be taken into consideration. Women at risk of being carriers should have their status determined prior to actively seeking conception. For autosomal-recessive disorders, paternal testing may be indicated as well. Carrier state and the risk of her fetus should be determined early in pregnancy by genetic testing. Chorionic villus sampling for diagnosis of hemophilia and other inherited bleeding disorders can be performed between 11 and 14 weeks of pregnancy. Amniocentesis can be done between the 15th and 20th week of pregnancy; both carry a risk of miscarriage between 1% and 2%.1 For X-linked recessive disorders, fetal sex determination can be performed in the first trimester by real-time polymerase chain reaction identification of Y-chromosome–specific sequences using cell-free fetal DNA in maternal plasma for genetic conditions affecting a particular sex such as hemophilia and may obviate the need for more invasive testing of a female fetus.2 Umbilical cord blood testing should be obtained at the time of delivery to avoid venipuncture and ensure early testing. von Willebrand disease Despite autosomal inheritance, women are more commonly diagnosed with von Willebrand disease (VWD) because of presentation at menarche or postpartum bleeding. Normally, factor VIII (FVIII) and von Willebrand factor (VWF) increase throughout pregnancy, sharply during the third trimester. For this reason, most patients with type 1 and some patients with type 2 VWD do not require prophylactic administration of concentrates prior to delivery. However, levels fall sharply immediately following delivery, by as much as 29%,3 and there is a considerable risk of postpartum hemorrhage and late bleeding. Bleeding may occur late and patients should be counseled to report heavy bleeding which may occur for a month or more postpartum. Patients with type 3 VWD and FVIII levels that are low or unmeasurable will require replacement at the time of delivery to prevent hemorrhage and should continue to receive replacement therapy 3 to 4 times daily for at least 3 to 5 days or longer.4 FVIII levels are considered the best predictors of bleeding risk and FVIII levels should be tested early in the third trimester and again later in the third trimester if levels are low, and monitored for 1 to 2 weeks after delivery. Bleeding risk decreases significantly at FVIII levels above 40 U/dL5 and factor replacement should be given along with VWF replacement at the time of delivery if factor levels are <50 U/dL.6 Plasma-derived VWF-containing concentrates should be infused to increase FVIII and VWF levels and maintain them at >50 U/dL. Vonvendi, recombinant VWF, was approved in late 2015.7 The use of desmopressin (DDAVP) antepartum is controversial because of a theoretical risk of vasoconstriction and placental insufficiency. DDAVP may be associated with hyponatremia and seizure, and tachyphylaxis occurs after repeated dosing due to depletion of endothelial stores. DDAVP is sometimes administered to patients with type 1 VWD at delivery, particularly with caesarean section and for several days afterward. Patients with type 2B VWD may develop severe thrombocytopenia, and are at risk of a fall in platelets. node_outputs.N8:
Recommended diagnostic steps for von Willebrand Disease

The diagnostic process for von Willebrand Disease (VWD) is guided by a stepwise algorithm that begins with clinical suspicion and progresses to targeted laboratory testing. The ASH ISTH NHF WFH 2021 guidelines emphasize that no single test is sufficient and that bleeding-assessment tools and diagnostic assays are central to diagnosis [N1-R3]. The recommended approach is therefore to combine history, bleeding phenotype, and a sequence of screening tests before subtype-specific assays are used [N1-R3].

Initial history and bleeding phenotype that suggest VWD
The guidelines note that suspicion of VWD arises when there is a family history of bleeding disorders, a history of mucocutaneous bleeding, or a bleeding phenotype that is inconsistent with hemophilia [N1-F1]. In pregnancy-specific care, the relevant history should also include a history of menorrhagia, epistaxis, easy bruising, or postpartum bleeding, because these symptoms are especially common in women with VWD [N1-F1]. The 2023 management guidance for pregnant women with bleeding disorders states that VWD is the most commonly encountered inherited bleeding disorder during pregnancy, aside from perhaps a mild undiagnosed platelet disorder [N4-R4]. This makes bleeding history especially important in the prenatal and obstetric setting.

Recommended screening tests for suspected cases
The diagnostic algorithm recommends starting with assays that measure VWF antigen (VWF:Ag), VWF activity, and factor VIII (FVIII) [N2-R2]. The guidelines also emphasize that VWF:Ag and FVIII:C are important diagnostic evaluations in the diagnosis of VWD, because individuals with type 1 or type 2 may have lower levels of FVIII:C [N2-R3]. In practice, this means the initial workup should include a VWF:Ag assay and FVIII:C assay, with VWF activity also being a key component of the diagnostic workup [N2-R2].

When to perform type-specific assays such as ristocetin cofactor and factor VIII activity
Type-specific assays are used after the initial screening phase to classify VWD into subtypes. The guidelines and diagnostic resources indicate that ristocetin cofactor activity is particularly useful in distinguishing between type 1 and type 2 VWD [N2-R5]. The ristocetin cofactor test measures the functional ability of VWF to bind platelets and is used to identify qualitative defects, while factor VIII activity is used to assess the functional consequences of VWF deficiency [N2-R3]. The 2023 management article also notes that type 2B VWD can result in severe thrombocytopenia and may require specific hemostatic management [N4-F2]. Therefore, type-specific assays are reserved for cases where the clinical phenotype and initial screening tests are not sufficient to classify the disorder [N1-F1][N2-R5].

Contextual background from pregnancy
Pregnancy-related changes can complicate interpretation of VWD screening tests. VWF and FVIII increase significantly during pregnancy in normal women, often reaching levels far above normal by the time of parturition [N5-R1][N5-F3]. This means that a normal or even elevated VWF:Ag and FVIII:C can occur in a pregnant woman with underlying VWD, especially type 1, and may mask a true deficiency [N5-F3]. In this context, the guideline-based diagnostic approach must be interpreted cautiously: screening tests should be repeated or interpreted alongside clinical history and bleeding phenotype, because pregnancy can normalize or falsely elevate test results [N5-F3]. This is important because the guidelines stress that diagnosis requires careful evaluation in pregnant women to plan the most appropriate treatment at parturition [N5-F3].

Overall, the recommended diagnostic steps are:
1) clinical suspicion based on bleeding phenotype and family history;
2) initial screening with VWF:Ag, FVIII:C, and VWF activity;
3) use of ristocetin cofactor and factor VIII activity to classify the subtype;
4) interpretation in the context of pregnancy-related changes in VWF, FVIII, and platelet function [N1-F1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5][N5-F3].
node_outputs.N10:
Distinguishing type 1 from type 2 von Willebrand Disease

Laboratory features that distinguish type 1 from type 2
The most important distinction between type 1 and type 2 VWD is qualitative versus quantitative VWF deficiency. The diagnostic literature states that type 2 VWD variants are characterized by a disproportionate decrease in VWF activity, either in terms of platelet binding, FVIII binding, or collagen binding [N2-R1]. In contrast, type 1 VWD is a partial quantitative deficiency, while type 2 is a qualitative defect that may be subdivided into subtypes A, B, M, and N [N4-F2]. A useful clinical laboratory feature is the VWF:RCo/VWF:Ag ratio: abnormal ratios, especially <0.6, are typically associated with type 2 VWD [N5-F3]. The ristocetin cofactor assay is specifically useful for detecting qualitative defects because a low vWF:RCo activity suggests either a quantitative deficiency (type 1 or 3) or a qualitative defect (type 2) [N2-R5]. Factor VIII activity is also important because individuals with type 1 or type 2 may have lower FVIII:C levels, and FVIII:C is an important diagnostic evaluation in the diagnosis of VWD [N2-R3].

How pregnancy can mask or mimic type 2 disease
Pregnancy can obscure the diagnosis of type 2 VWD because VWF and FVIII increase significantly during pregnancy in normal women, and some women with type 2 VWD may achieve normal or near-normal levels during pregnancy [N5-R1][N5-F3]. The literature reports that women with abnormal VWF:RCo/VWF:Ag ratios at baseline—often indicative of type 2 VWD—maintain the abnormality throughout pregnancy and often do not reach safe levels ≥50 U/dL [N5-F3]. However, other women with type 2 VWD may have higher VWF:Ag and FVIII:C levels during pregnancy, making the defect harder to detect by routine screening tests alone. This means that pregnancy can mask a type 2 diagnosis, especially in women whose baseline VWF:Ag and FVIII:C are already low [N5-F3]. Conversely, pregnancy can also mimic a normal result in a woman with type 2 VWD who has a transient improvement in VWF and FVIII levels, which may lead to overconfidence in a negative diagnosis [N5-F3].

Clinical implications of type classification for management
The clinical implications of type classification are substantial because management differs depending on the subtype. The guidelines emphasize that diagnosis and subtype classification are essential for appropriate management [N1-F1]. For type 1 VWD, the main concern is that pregnancy can normalize or falsely elevate screening tests, so treatment may not be needed before delivery if VWF and FVIII levels are adequate [N5-F3]. In contrast, type 2 VWD, especially type 2B, may require more aggressive management because these patients may develop severe thrombocytopenia and may not respond well to desmopressin [N4-F2]. The literature also notes that type 2N VWD results from gain-of-function mutations producing a variant VWF with abnormally increased affinity for the platelet GPIb receptor, and this variant may behave differently than other type 2 subtypes [N5-R5]. Therefore, type classification affects both the choice of therapy during pregnancy and the need for replacement therapy, especially when baseline VWF:RCo/VWF:Ag ratios are abnormal [N5-F3][N4-F2].

In short, type 1 VWD is primarily a quantitative defect, while type 2 is a qualitative defect with subtype-specific laboratory features; pregnancy can mask type 2 disease or make its diagnosis more difficult; and the type classification directly determines the management plan, including replacement therapy, desmopressin use, and thrombocytopenia monitoring [N2-R1][N2-R5][N4-F2][N5-F3].
node_outputs.N9:
How pregnancy changes the diagnostic landscape for VWD

How pregnancy alters VWF, FVIII, and platelet function
Pregnancy alters VWF, FVIII, and platelet function in ways that can complicate diagnosis. The evidence shows that VWF and FVIII increase significantly during pregnancy, often reaching levels far above normal by the time of parturition [N5-R1][N5-F3]. Normal women may already have elevated levels in the first trimester, and the increases are even greater in the last trimester [N5-R3]. This means that pregnancy can normalize or falsely elevate screening tests for VWD, especially VWF:Ag and FVIII:C. In addition, platelet function changes during pregnancy, with the PFA-100 and other platelet-function tests being used in clinical practice, though they lack sensitivity and specificity and are not disease-specific [N7-R1][N7-R2]. The literature also notes that platelet number and function are affected by pregnancy, which can influence bleeding phenotype and test interpretation [N7-R1][N7-R3].

How pregnancy can normalize or falsely elevate test results
Pregnancy-related increases in VWF and FVIII can normalize the test results in patients with type 1 VWD, making the diagnosis less obvious [N5-F3]. The same evidence also states that women with baseline VWF and FVIII levels >30 U/dL have a high likelihood of achieving normal levels at the end of pregnancy, so specific anti-hemorrhagic prophylaxis is seldom required [N5-F3]. This is important because a normal or elevated VWF:Ag and FVIII:C may occur in a pregnant woman with underlying VWD, especially type 1, and may falsely suggest that the bleeding disorder is not present [N5-F3]. In contrast, women with baseline levels <20 U/dL may not respond well to pregnancy-related increases, and some may have mutations associated with increased VWF clearance or compound heterozygosity, which prevent the achievement of satisfactory hemostatic levels [N5-F3]. This means that pregnancy can both mask a true deficiency and create false reassurance.

How to interpret test results during pregnancy versus nonpregnancy
Because pregnancy alters hemostatic parameters, test results must be interpreted in the context of gestational age and physiological changes. The guidelines emphasize that diagnosis requires careful evaluation of pregnant women because pregnancy can normalize or falsely elevate test results [N5-F3]. This implies that VWF:Ag and FVIII:C should not be used in isolation during pregnancy; instead, they should be interpreted alongside clinical bleeding phenotype and other laboratory findings [N5-F3]. The literature also suggests that the VWF:RCo/VWF:Ag ratio is especially informative because abnormal ratios are typically associated with type 2 VWD, and these ratios may be maintained during pregnancy [N5-F3]. Therefore, the diagnostic approach in pregnancy should be adjusted to account for the fact that:
- VWF and FVIII may rise substantially;
- platelet function tests are not specific;
- baseline deficiencies may be masked or exaggerated;
- subtype-specific assays remain important but must be interpreted cautiously [N5-F3][N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R3].

Overall, pregnancy changes the diagnostic landscape for VWD by raising VWF and FVIII levels, altering platelet function, and potentially normalizing or falsely elevating test results. This means that test interpretation during pregnancy should be more cautious than during nonpregnancy, and subtype-specific assays should be used only when the clinical and laboratory findings are inconclusive [N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-F3][N7-R1][N7-R2].
node_outputs.N11:
Diagnostic pitfalls and differential diagnosis during pregnancy

Limitations of routine tests and pitfalls in interpretation
Routine tests have important limitations during pregnancy. Platelet function tests, including bleeding time and the PFA-100, are not disease-specific and lack sensitivity and specificity [N3-R1][N7-R1][N7-R2]. Distinguishing type 1 from type 2 von Willebrand Disease

Laboratory features that distinguish type 1 from type 2
The most important distinction between type 1 and type 2 VWD is qualitative versus quantitative VWF deficiency. The diagnostic literature states that type 2 VWD variants are characterized by a disproportionate decrease in VWF activity, either in terms of platelet binding, FVIII binding, or collagen binding [N2-R1]. In contrast, type 1 VWD is a partial quantitative deficiency, while type 2 is a qualitative defect that may be subdivided into subtypes A, B, M, and N [N4-F2]. A useful clinical laboratory feature is the VWF:RCo/VWF:Ag ratio: abnormal ratios, especially <0.6, are typically associated with type 2 VWD [N5-F3]. The ristocetin cofactor assay is specifically useful for detecting qualitative defects because a low vWF:RCo activity suggests either a quantitative deficiency (type 1 or 3) or a qualitative defect (type 2) [N2-R5]. Factor VIII activity is also important because individuals with type 1 or type 2 may have lower FVIII:C levels, and FVIII:C is an important diagnostic evaluation in the diagnosis of VWD [N2-R3].

How pregnancy can mask or mimic type 2 disease
Pregnancy can obscure the diagnosis of type 2 VWD because VWF and FVIII increase significantly during pregnancy in normal women, and some women with type 2 VWD may achieve normal or near-normal levels during pregnancy [N5-R1][N5-F3]. The literature reports that women with abnormal VWF:RCo/VWF:Ag ratios at baseline—often indicative of type 2 VWD—maintain the abnormality throughout pregnancy and often do not reach safe levels ≥50 U/dL [N5-F3]. However, other women with type 2 VWD may have higher VWF:Ag and FVIII:C levels during pregnancy, making the defect harder to detect by routine screening tests alone. This means that pregnancy can mask a type 2 diagnosis, especially in women whose baseline VWF:Ag and FVIII:C are already low [N5-F3]. Conversely, pregnancy can also mimic a normal result in a woman with type 2 VWD who has a transient improvement in VWF and FVIII levels, which may lead to overconfidence in a negative diagnosis [N5-F3].

The clinical implications of type classification are substantial because management differs depending on the subtype. The guidelines emphasize that diagnosis and subtype classification are essential for appropriate management [N1-F1]. For type 1 VWD, the main concern is that pregnancy can normalize or falsely elevate screening tests, so treatment may not be needed before delivery if VWF and FVIII levels are adequate [N5-F3]. How pregnancy changes the diagnostic landscape for VWD

How pregnancy alters VWF, FVIII, and platelet function
Pregnancy alters VWF, FVIII, and platelet function in ways that can complicate diagnosis. The evidence shows that VWF and FVIII increase significantly during pregnancy, often reaching levels far above normal by the time of parturition [N5-R1][N5-F3]. Normal women may already have elevated levels in the first trimester, and the increases are even greater in the last trimester [N5-R3]. This means that pregnancy can normalize or falsely elevate screening tests for VWD, especially VWF:Ag and FVIII:C. In addition, platelet function changes during pregnancy, with the PFA-100 and other platelet-function tests being used in clinical practice, though they lack sensitivity and specificity and are not disease-specific [N7-R1][N7-R2]. The literature also notes that platelet number and function are affected by pregnancy, which can influence bleeding phenotype and test interpretation [N7-R1][N7-R3].

How pregnancy can normalize or falsely elevate test results
Pregnancy-related increases in VWF and FVIII can normalize the test results in patients with type 1 VWD, making the diagnosis less obvious [N5-F3]. The same evidence also states that women with baseline VWF and FVIII levels >30 U/dL have a high likelihood of achieving normal levels at the end of pregnancy, so specific anti-hemorrhagic prophylaxis is seldom required [N5-F3]. This is important because a normal or elevated VWF:Ag and FVIII:C may occur in a pregnant woman with underlying VWD, especially type 1, and may falsely suggest that the bleeding disorder is not present [N5-F3]. In contrast, women with baseline levels <20 U/dL may not respond well to pregnancy-related increases, and some may have mutations associated with increased VWF clearance or compound heterozygosity, which prevent the achievement of satisfactory hemostatic levels [N5-F3]. This means that pregnancy can both mask a true deficiency and create false reassurance.

How to interpret test results during pregnancy versus nonpregnancy
Because pregnancy alters hemostatic parameters, test results must be interpreted in the context of gestational age and physiological changes. The guidelines emphasize that diagnosis requires careful evaluation of pregnant women because pregnancy can normalize or falsely elevate test results [N5-F3]. This implies that VWF:Ag and FVIII:C should not be used in isolation during pregnancy; instead, they should be interpreted alongside clinical bleeding phenotype and other laboratory findings [N5-F3]. The literature also suggests that the VWF:RCo/VWF:Ag ratio is especially informative because abnormal ratios are typically associated with type 2 VWD, and these ratios may be maintained during pregnancy [N5-F3]. Therefore, the diagnostic approach in pregnancy should be adjusted to account for the fact that:
- VWF and FVIII may rise substantially;
- platelet function tests are not specific;
- baseline deficiencies may be masked or exaggerated;
- subtype-specific assays remain important but must be interpreted cautiously [N5-F3][N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R3].

Overall, pregnancy changes the diagnostic landscape for VWD by raising VWF and FVIII levels, altering platelet function, and potentially normalizing or falsely elevating test results. This means that test interpretation during pregnancy should be more cautious than during nonpregnancy, and subtype-specific assays should be used only when the clinical and laboratory findings are inconclusive [N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-F3][N7-R1][N7-R2].

Diagnostic pitfalls and differential diagnosis during pregnancy

Limitations of routine tests and pitfalls in interpretation
Routine tests have important limitations during pregnancy. Platelet function tests, including bleeding time and the PFA-100, are not disease-specific and lack sensitivity and specificity [N3-R1][N7-R1][N7-R2]. The literature also reports that discrepancies between platelet-function tests are common, with most studies finding that the PFA test and template bleeding time give equivalent results in about 75% of cases [N7-R3]. This means that routine platelet-function testing is not reliable enough to distinguish VWD from other bleeding disorders or from normal pregnancy-related changes. Similarly, bleeding time is noted to lack sensitivity and specificity, and it is not a reliable first-line test [N7-R4]. The ASH 2023 guidance on pregnant women with bleeding disorders further states that inherited bleeding disorders are common during pregnancy, and diagnostic challenges arise because acquired disorders can present particular difficulties [N3-R2]. Therefore, the main pitfalls are:
- reliance on non-specific platelet-function tests;
- underestimation of the true bleeding risk because tests can be normal or falsely elevated;
- difficulty distinguishing between inherited and acquired defects [N3-R1][N7-R1][N7-R2][N3-R2].

Differential diagnosis of inherited versus acquired bleeding disorders
During pregnancy, the differential diagnosis must include both inherited and acquired bleeding disorders. The literature emphasizes that congenital and acquired bleeding disorders may present diagnostic difficulties and require rapid diagnosis and management [N3-R2]. Inherited disorders are especially important because VWD is the most commonly encountered inherited bleeding disorder during pregnancy [N4-R4]. Acquired disorders may include thrombocytopenia, liver disease, or other conditions that affect hemostasis [N3-R2][N3-R4]. The management guidance also notes that acquired abnormalities of hemostasis may present particular difficulties with diagnosis and management [N3-R2]. In this setting, the differential diagnosis should therefore include:
- inherited disorders such as VWD, hemophilia A, hemophilia B, and other inherited platelet-function disorders;
- acquired disorders that may occur with pregnancy, including thrombocytopenia and other acquired coagulopathy [N3-R2][N3-R4][N6-R3].

Special considerations for maternal bleeding risk and fetal safety
Maternal bleeding risk and fetal safety are central to the differential diagnosis. The literature states that inherited bleeding disorders increase bleeding risk during pregnancy, childbirth, and the postpartum period [N6-R5]. In pregnancy-specific care, the focus is not only on maternal safety but also on fetal safety, because bleeding disorders may have significant implications for the fetus and neonate [N6-F4]. The congenital-and-acquired bleeding-disorders article notes that women with congenital bleeding disorders or who are carriers should be counseled prior to conception and followed closely during pregnancy, through delivery, and in the immediate postpartum period [N6-F4]. It also emphasizes that the risk of the fetus inheriting the bleeding tendency must be considered, and prenatal diagnosis may be performed with chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis [N6-F4]. This means that differential diagnosis during pregnancy must include not only the immediate bleeding disorder but also the possibility of a hereditary condition affecting the fetus. The pregnancy-specific management guidance further notes that maternal bleeding complications may require blood transfusion, and that specialized care involving hematologists, obstetricians, and anesthesiologists is essential [N6-F4]. Therefore, the diagnostic process must balance maternal bleeding risk with fetal safety and ensure that prenatal diagnosis and counseling are part of the care plan [N6-F4][N6-R1].

In summary, the diagnostic pitfalls during pregnancy include reliance on non-specific platelet-function tests and the possibility of false normalization or elevation of test results [N3-R1][N7-R1][N7-R2]. The differential diagnosis must include both inherited disorders such as VWD and acquired disorders that may occur with pregnancy [N3-R2][N3-R4][N6-R3]. Special considerations are maternal bleeding risk and fetal safety, with prenatal diagnosis and specialized multidisciplinary management being essential [N6-F4][N6-R1].

Recommended diagnostic steps for von Willebrand Disease

The diagnostic process for von Willebrand Disease (VWD) is guided by a stepwise algorithm that begins with clinical suspicion and progresses to targeted laboratory testing. The ASH ISTH NHF WFH 2021 guidelines emphasize that no single test is sufficient and that bleeding-assessment tools and diagnostic assays are central to diagnosis [N1-R3]. The recommended approach is therefore to combine history, bleeding phenotype, and a sequence of screening tests before subtype-specific assays are used [N1-R3].

Initial history and bleeding phenotype that suggest VWD
The guidelines note that suspicion of VWD arises when there is a family history of bleeding disorders, a history of mucocutaneous bleeding, or a bleeding phenotype that is inconsistent with hemophilia [N1-F1]. In pregnancy-specific care, the relevant history should also include a history of menorrhagia, epistaxis, easy bruising, or postpartum bleeding, because these symptoms are especially common in women with VWD [N1-F1]. The 2023 management guidance for pregnant women with bleeding disorders states that VWD is the most commonly encountered inherited bleeding disorder during pregnancy, aside from perhaps a mild undiagnosed platelet disorder [N4-R4]. This makes bleeding history especially important in the prenatal and obstetric setting.

Recommended screening tests for suspected cases
The diagnostic algorithm recommends starting with assays that measure VWF antigen (VWF:Ag), VWF activity, and factor VIII (FVIII) [N2-R2]. The guidelines also emphasize that VWF:Ag and FVIII:C are important diagnostic evaluations in the diagnosis of VWD, because individuals with type 1 or type 2 may have lower levels of FVIII:C [N2-R3]. In practice, this means the initial workup should include a VWF:Ag assay and FVIII:C assay, with VWF activity also being a key component of the diagnostic workup [N2-R2].

When to perform type-specific assays such as ristocetin cofactor and factor VIII activity
Type-specific assays are used after the initial screening phase to classify VWD into subtypes. The guidelines and diagnostic resources indicate that ristocetin cofactor activity is particularly useful in distinguishing between type 1 and type 2 VWD [N2-R5]. The ristocetin cofactor test measures the functional ability of VWF to bind platelets and is used to identify qualitative defects, while factor VIII activity is used to assess the functional consequences of VWF deficiency [N2-R3]. The 2023 management article also notes that type 2B VWD can result in severe thrombocytopenia and may require specific hemostatic management [N4-F2]. Therefore, type-specific assays are reserved for cases where the clinical phenotype and initial screening tests are not sufficient to classify the disorder [N1-F1][N2-R5].

Contextual background from pregnancy
Pregnancy-related changes can complicate interpretation of VWD screening tests. VWF and FVIII increase significantly during pregnancy in normal women, often reaching levels far above normal by the time of parturition [N5-R1][N5-F3]. This means that a normal or even elevated VWF:Ag and FVIII:C can occur in a pregnant woman with underlying VWD, especially type 1, and may mask a true deficiency [N5-F3]. In this context, the guideline-based diagnostic approach must be interpreted cautiously: screening tests should be repeated or interpreted alongside clinical history and bleeding phenotype, because pregnancy can normalize or falsely elevate test results [N5-F3]. This is important because the guidelines stress that diagnosis requires careful evaluation in pregnant women to plan the most appropriate treatment at parturition [N5-F3].

Overall, the recommended diagnostic steps are:
1) clinical suspicion based on bleeding phenotype and family history;
2) initial screening with VWF:Ag, FVIII:C, and VWF activity;
3) use of ristocetin cofactor and factor VIII activity to classify the subtype;
4) interpretation in the context of pregnancy-related changes in VWF, FVIII, and platelet function [N1-F1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R5][N5-F3].

Distinguishing type 1 from type 2 von Willebrand Disease

Laboratory features that distinguish type 1 from type 2
The most important distinction between type 1 and type 2 VWD is qualitative versus quantitative VWF deficiency. The diagnostic literature states that type 2 VWD variants are characterized by a disproportionate decrease in VWF activity, either in terms of platelet binding, FVIII binding, or collagen binding [N2-R1]. In contrast, type 1 VWD is a partial quantitative deficiency, while type 2 is a qualitative defect that may be subdivided into subtypes A, B, M, and N [N4-F2]. A useful clinical laboratory feature is the VWF:RCo/VWF:Ag ratio: abnormal ratios, especially <0.6, are typically associated with type 2 VWD [N5-F3]. The ristocetin cofactor assay is specifically useful for detecting qualitative defects because a low vWF:RCo activity suggests either a quantitative deficiency (type 1 or 3) or a qualitative defect (type 2) [N2-R5]. Factor VIII activity is also important because individuals with type 1 or type 2 may have lower FVIII:C levels, and FVIII:C is an important diagnostic evaluation in the diagnosis of VWD [N2-R3].

How pregnancy can mask or mimic type 2 disease
Pregnancy can obscure the diagnosis of type 2 VWD because VWF and FVIII increase significantly during pregnancy in normal women, and some women with type 2 VWD may achieve normal or near-normal levels during pregnancy [N5-R1][N5-F3]. The literature reports that women with abnormal VWF:RCo/VWF:Ag ratios at baseline—often indicative of type 2 VWD—maintain the abnormality throughout pregnancy and often do not reach safe levels ≥50 U/dL [N5-F3]. However, other women with type 2 VWD may have higher VWF:Ag and FVIII:C levels during pregnancy, making the defect harder to detect by routine screening tests alone. This means that pregnancy can mask a type 2 diagnosis, especially in women whose baseline VWF:Ag and FVIII:C are already low [N5-F3]. Conversely, pregnancy can also mimic a normal result in a woman with type 2 VWD who has a transient improvement in VWF and FVIII levels, which may lead to overconfidence in a negative diagnosis [N5-F3].

Clinical implications of type classification for management
The clinical implications of type classification are substantial because management differs depending on the subtype. The guidelines emphasize that diagnosis and subtype classification are essential for appropriate management [N1-F1]. For type 1 VWD, the main concern is that pregnancy can normalize or falsely elevate screening tests, so treatment may not be needed before delivery if VWF and FVIII levels are adequate [N5-F3]. In contrast, type 2 VWD, especially type 2B, may require more aggressive management because these patients may develop severe thrombocytopenia and may not respond well to desmopressin [N4-F2]. The literature also notes that type 2N VWD results from gain-of-function mutations producing a variant VWF with abnormally increased affinity for the platelet GPIb receptor, and this variant may behave differently than other type 2 subtypes [N5-R5]. Therefore, type classification affects both the choice of therapy during pregnancy and the need for replacement therapy, especially when baseline VWF:RCo/VWF:Ag ratios are abnormal [N5-F3][N4-F2].

In short, type 1 VWD is primarily a quantitative defect, while type 2 is a qualitative defect with subtype-specific laboratory features; pregnancy can mask type 2 disease or make its diagnosis more difficult; and the type classification directly determines the management plan, including replacement therapy, desmopressin use, and thrombocytopenia monitoring [N2-R1][N2-R5][N4-F2][N5-F3].
branch_outputs.N9:
How pregnancy changes the diagnostic landscape for VWD

How pregnancy alters VWF, FVIII, and platelet function
Pregnancy alters VWF, FVIII, and platelet function in ways that can complicate diagnosis. The evidence shows that VWF and FVIII increase significantly during pregnancy, often reaching levels far above normal by the time of parturition [N5-R1][N5-F3]. Normal women may already have elevated levels in the first trimester, and the increases are even greater in the last trimester [N5-R3]. This means that pregnancy can normalize or falsely elevate screening tests for VWD, especially VWF:Ag and FVIII:C. In addition, platelet function changes during pregnancy, with the PFA-100 and other platelet-function tests being used in clinical practice, though they lack sensitivity and specificity and are not disease-specific [N7-R1][N7-R2]. The literature also notes that platelet number and function are affected by pregnancy, which can influence bleeding phenotype and test interpretation [N7-R1][N7-R3].

How pregnancy can normalize or falsely elevate test results
Pregnancy-related increases in VWF and FVIII can normalize the test results in patients with type 1 VWD, making the diagnosis less obvious [N5-F3]. The same evidence also states that women with baseline VWF and FVIII levels >30 U/dL have a high likelihood of achieving normal levels at the end of pregnancy, so specific anti-hemorrhagic prophylaxis is seldom required [N5-F3]. This is important because a normal or elevated VWF:Ag and FVIII:C may occur in a pregnant woman with underlying VWD, especially type 1, and may falsely suggest that the bleeding disorder is not present [N5-F3]. In contrast, women with baseline levels <20 U/dL may not respond well to pregnancy-related increases, and some may have mutations associated with increased VWF clearance or compound heterozygosity, which prevent the achievement of satisfactory hemostatic levels [N5-F3]. This means that pregnancy can both mask a true deficiency and create false reassurance.

How to interpret test results during pregnancy versus nonpregnancy
Because pregnancy alters hemostatic parameters, test results must be interpreted in the context of gestational age and physiological changes. The guidelines emphasize that diagnosis requires careful evaluation of pregnant women because pregnancy can normalize or falsely elevate test results [N5-F3]. This implies that VWF:Ag and FVIII:C should not be used in isolation during pregnancy; instead, they should be interpreted alongside clinical bleeding phenotype and other laboratory findings [N5-F3]. The literature also suggests that the VWF:RCo/VWF:Ag ratio is especially informative because abnormal ratios are typically associated with type 2 VWD, and these ratios may be maintained during pregnancy [N5-F3]. Therefore, the diagnostic approach in pregnancy should be adjusted to account for the fact that:
- VWF and FVIII may rise substantially;
- platelet function tests are not specific;
- baseline deficiencies may be masked or exaggerated;
- subtype-specific assays remain important but must be interpreted cautiously [N5-F3][N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R3].

Overall, pregnancy changes the diagnostic landscape for VWD by raising VWF and FVIII levels, altering platelet function, and potentially normalizing or falsely elevating test results. This means that test interpretation during pregnancy should be more cautious than during nonpregnancy, and subtype-specific assays should be used only when the clinical and laboratory findings are inconclusive [N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-F3][N7-R1][N7-R2].
branch_outputs.N11:
Diagnostic pitfalls and differential diagnosis during pregnancy

Limitations of routine tests and pitfalls in interpretation
Routine tests have important limitations during pregnancy. Platelet function tests, including bleeding time and the PFA-100, are not disease-specific and lack sensitivity and specificity [N3-R1][N7-R1][N7-R2]. The literature also reports that discrepancies between platelet-function tests are common, with most studies finding that the PFA test and template bleeding time give equivalent results in about 75% of cases [N7-R3]. This means that routine platelet-function testing is not reliable enough to distinguish VWD from other bleeding disorders or from normal pregnancy-related changes. Similarly, bleeding time is noted to lack sensitivity and specificity, and it is not a reliable first-line test [N7-R4]. The ASH 2023 guidance on pregnant women with bleeding disorders further states that inherited bleeding disorders are common during pregnancy, and diagnostic challenges arise because acquired disorders can present particular difficulties [N3-R2]. Therefore, the main pitfalls are:
- reliance on non-specific platelet-function tests;
- underestimation of the true bleeding risk because tests can be normal or falsely elevated;
- difficulty distinguishing between inherited and acquired defects [N3-R1][N7-R1][N7-R2][N3-R2].

Differential diagnosis of inherited versus acquired bleeding disorders
During pregnancy, the differential diagnosis must include both inherited and acquired bleeding disorders. The literature emphasizes that congenital and acquired bleeding disorders may present diagnostic difficulties and require rapid diagnosis and management [N3-R2]. Inherited disorders are especially important because VWD is the most commonly encountered inherited bleeding disorder during pregnancy [N4-R4]. Acquired disorders may include thrombocytopenia, liver disease, or other conditions that affect hemostasis [N3-R2][N3-R4]. The management guidance also notes that acquired abnormalities of hemostasis may present particular difficulties with diagnosis and management [N3-R2]. In this setting, the differential diagnosis should therefore include:
- inherited disorders such as VWD, hemophilia A, hemophilia B, and other inherited platelet-function disorders;
- acquired disorders that may occur with pregnancy, including thrombocytopenia and other acquired coagulopathy [N3-R2][N3-R4][N6-R3].

Special considerations for maternal bleeding risk and fetal safety
Maternal bleeding risk and fetal safety are central to the differential diagnosis. The literature states that inherited bleeding disorders increase bleeding risk during pregnancy, childbirth, and the postpartum period [N6-R5]. In pregnancy-specific care, the focus is not only on maternal safety but also on fetal safety, because bleeding disorders may have significant implications for the fetus and neonate [N6-F4]. The congenital-and-acquired bleeding-disorders article notes that women with congenital bleeding disorders or who are carriers should be counseled prior to conception and followed closely during pregnancy, through delivery, and in the immediate postpartum period [N6-F4]. It also emphasizes that the risk of the fetus inheriting the bleeding tendency must be considered, and prenatal diagnosis may be performed with chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis [N6-F4]. This means that differential diagnosis during pregnancy must include not only the immediate bleeding disorder but also the possibility of a hereditary condition affecting the fetus. The pregnancy-specific management guidance further notes that maternal bleeding complications may require blood transfusion, and that specialized care involving hematologists, obstetricians, and anesthesiologists is essential [N6-F4]. Therefore, the diagnostic process must balance maternal bleeding risk with fetal safety and ensure that prenatal diagnosis and counseling are part of the care plan [N6-F4][N6-R1].

In summary, the diagnostic pitfalls during pregnancy include reliance on non-specific platelet-function tests and the possibility of false normalization or elevation of test results [N3-R1][N7-R1][N7-R2]. The differential diagnosis must include both inherited disorders such as VWD and acquired disorders that may occur with pregnancy [N3-R2][N3-R4][N6-R3]. Special considerations are maternal bleeding risk and fetal safety, with prenatal diagnosis and specialized multidisciplinary management being essential [N6-F4][N6-R1].

During pregnancy, the differential diagnosis must include both inherited and acquired bleeding disorders. - inherited disorders such as VWD, hemophilia A, hemophilia B, and other inherited platelet-function disorders;
- acquired disorders that may occur with pregnancy, including thrombocytopenia and other acquired coagulopathy [N3-R2][N3-R4][N6-R3].

Overall, the recommended diagnostic steps for VWD are clear and evidence-based, but pregnancy introduces major challenges. ### 1) Initial clinical suspicion and bleeding phenotype
The first step in diagnosing von Willebrand Disease (VWD) is clinical suspicion based on the patient’s history and bleeding phenotype. The guidelines emphasize that suspicion arises when there is a family history of bleeding disorders, mucocutaneous bleeding, or a bleeding phenotype inconsistent with hemophilia [N1-F1]. During pregnancy, the relevant history should also include menorrhagia, epistaxis, easy bruising, or postpartum bleeding, because these symptoms are especially common in women with VWD [N1-F1]. The 2023 management guidance further states that VWD is the most commonly encountered inherited bleeding disorder during pregnancy, aside from perhaps a mild undiagnosed platelet disorder [N4-R4]. Therefore, a careful history is essential in the prenatal and obstetric setting.

### 2) Recommended screening tests for suspected cases
The diagnostic algorithm recommends starting with assays that measure VWF antigen (VWF:Ag), VWF activity, and factor VIII (FVIII) [N2-R2]. The guidelines also emphasize that VWF:Ag and FVIII:C are important diagnostic evaluations in the diagnosis of VWD, because individuals with type 1 or type 2 may have lower levels of FVIII:C [N2-R3]. In practice, this means the initial workup should include a VWF:Ag assay and FVIII:C assay, with VWF activity also being a key component of the diagnostic workup [N2-R2]. The 2023 management article also notes that type 2B VWD may develop severe thrombocytopenia and may require specific hemostatic management [N4-F2], highlighting the importance of early testing before delivery.

### 3) When to perform type-specific assays
Type-specific assays are used after the initial screening phase to classify VWD into subtypes. The guidelines and diagnostic resources indicate that ristocetin cofactor activity is particularly useful in distinguishing between type 1 and type 2 VWD [N2-R5]. The ristocetin cofactor test measures the functional ability of VWF to bind platelets and is used to identify qualitative defects, while factor VIII activity is used to assess the functional consequences of VWF deficiency [N2-R3]. Because VWD diagnosis requires careful evaluation, especially in pregnancy, these assays are reserved for cases where the clinical phenotype and initial screening tests are not sufficient to classify the disorder [N1-F1][N2-R5].

### 4) Pregnancy-related changes that complicate diagnosis
Pregnancy changes the diagnostic landscape for VWD in several important ways. VWF and FVIII increase significantly during pregnancy, often reaching levels far above normal by the time of parturition [N5-R1][N5-F3]. Normal women may already have elevated levels in the first trimester, and the increases are even greater in the last trimester [N5-R3]. This means that pregnancy can normalize or falsely elevate screening tests for VWD, especially VWF:Ag and FVIII:C [N5-F3]. In pregnancy-specific care, the guidelines emphasize that diagnosis requires careful evaluation because pregnancy can normalize or falsely elevate test results [N5-F3]. This is especially important because a normal or elevated VWF:Ag and FVIII:C may occur in a pregnant woman with underlying VWD, making the diagnosis less obvious [N5-F3].

### 5) How pregnancy can mask or mimic type 2 disease
Pregnancy can mask type 2 VWD because some women with type 2 VWD may achieve normal or near-normal VWF and FVIII levels during pregnancy, especially if they have abnormal VWF:RCo/VWF:Ag ratios at baseline [N5-F3]. The literature reports that women with abnormal VWF:RCo/VWF:Ag ratios typically associated with type 2 VWD maintain the abnormality throughout pregnancy and often do not reach safe levels ≥50 U/dL [N5-F3]. However, other women with type 2 VWD may have higher VWF:Ag and FVIII:C levels during pregnancy, making the defect harder to detect by routine screening tests alone [N5-F3]. This means that pregnancy can both mask a true deficiency and create false reassurance.

### 6) How to interpret test results during pregnancy versus nonpregnancy
Because pregnancy alters hemostatic parameters, test results must be interpreted in the context of gestational age and physiological changes. The guidelines emphasize that diagnosis requires careful evaluation of pregnant women because pregnancy can normalize or falsely elevate test results [N5-F3]. This implies that VWF:Ag and FVIII:C should not be used in isolation during pregnancy; instead, they should be interpreted alongside clinical bleeding phenotype and other laboratory findings [N5-F3]. The literature also suggests that the VWF:RCo/VWF:Ag ratio is especially informative because abnormal ratios are typically associated with type 2 VWD, and these ratios may be maintained during pregnancy [N5-F3]. Therefore, the diagnostic approach in pregnancy should be adjusted to account for the fact that:
- VWF and FVIII may rise substantially;
- platelet function tests are not specific;
- baseline deficiencies may be masked or exaggerated;
- subtype-specific assays remain important but must be interpreted cautiously [N5-F3][N7-R1][N7-R2].

### 7) Laboratory features distinguishing type 1 from type 2 VWD
The most important distinction between type 1 and type 2 VWD is qualitative versus quantitative VWF deficiency. Type 2 VWD variants are characterized by a disproportionate decrease in VWF activity, either in terms of platelet binding, FVIII binding, or collagen binding [N2-R1]. In contrast, type 1 is a partial quantitative deficiency, while type 2 is a qualitative defect that may be subdivided into subtypes A, B, M, and N [N4-F2]. A useful clinical laboratory feature is the VWF:RCo/VWF:Ag ratio: abnormal ratios, especially <0.6, are typically associated with type 2 VWD [N5-F3]. The ristocetin cofactor assay is specifically useful for detecting qualitative defects because a low vWF:RCo activity suggests either a quantitative deficiency (type 1 or 3) or a qualitative defect (type 2) [N2-R5]. Factor VIII activity is also important because individuals with type 1 or type 2 may have lower FVIII:C levels, and FVIII:C is an important diagnostic evaluation in the diagnosis of VWD [N2-R3].

### 8) Clinical implications of type classification for management
Type classification directly affects management. The guidelines emphasize that diagnosis and subtype classification are essential for appropriate management [N1-F1]. For type 1 VWD, pregnancy can normalize or falsely elevate screening tests, so treatment may not be needed before delivery if VWF and FVIII levels are adequate [N5-F3]. In contrast, type 2 VWD, especially type 2B, may require more aggressive management because these patients may develop severe thrombocytopenia and may not respond well to desmopressin [N4-F2]. The literature also notes that type 2N VWD results from gain-of-function mutations producing a variant VWF with abnormally increased affinity for the platelet GPIb receptor, and this variant may behave differently than other type 2 subtypes [N5-R5]. Therefore, type classification affects the choice of therapy during pregnancy, the need for replacement therapy, and the monitoring of thrombocytopenia [N2-R1][N2-R5][N4-F2][N5-F3].

### 9) Diagnostic pitfalls and limitations of routine tests
Routine tests have important limitations during pregnancy. Platelet-function tests, including bleeding time and the PFA-100, are not disease-specific and lack sensitivity and specificity [N3-R1][N7-R1][N7-R2]. The literature also reports that discrepancies between platelet-function tests are common, with most studies finding that the PFA test and template bleeding time give equivalent results in about 75% of cases [N7-R3]. This means that routine platelet-function testing is not reliable enough to distinguish VWD from other bleeding disorders or from normal pregnancy-related changes. Similarly, bleeding time is noted to lack sensitivity and specificity, and it is not a reliable first-line test [N7-R4]. The ASH 2023 guidance on pregnant women with bleeding disorders further states that inherited bleeding disorders are common during pregnancy, and diagnostic challenges arise because acquired disorders can present particular difficulties [N3-R2]. Therefore, the main pitfalls are:
- reliance on non-specific platelet-function tests;
- underestimation of the true bleeding risk because tests can be normal or falsely elevated;
- difficulty distinguishing between inherited and acquired defects [N3-R1][N7-R1][N7-R2][N3-R2].

### 10) Differential diagnosis of inherited versus acquired bleeding disorders
During pregnancy, the differential diagnosis must include both inherited and acquired bleeding disorders. The literature emphasizes that congenital and acquired bleeding disorders may present diagnostic difficulties and require rapid diagnosis and management [N3-R2]. Inherited disorders are especially important because VWD is the most commonly encountered inherited bleeding disorder during pregnancy [N4-R4]. Acquired disorders may include thrombocytopenia, liver disease, or other conditions that affect hemostasis [N3-R2][N3-R4]. The management guidance also notes that acquired abnormalities of hemostasis may present particular difficulties with diagnosis and management [N3-R2]. In this setting, the differential diagnosis should therefore include:
- inherited disorders such as VWD, hemophilia A, hemophilia B, and other inherited platelet-function disorders;
- acquired disorders that may occur with pregnancy, including thrombocytopenia and other acquired coagulopathy [N3-R2][N3-R4][N6-R3].

### 11) Special considerations for maternal bleeding risk and fetal safety
Maternal bleeding risk and fetal safety are central to the differential diagnosis. The literature states that inherited bleeding disorders increase bleeding risk during pregnancy, childbirth, and the postpartum period [N6-R5]. In pregnancy-specific care, the focus is not only on maternal safety but also on fetal safety, because bleeding disorders may have significant implications for the fetus and neonate [N6-F4]. The congenital-and-acquired bleeding-disorders article notes that women with congenital bleeding disorders or who are carriers should be counseled prior to conception and followed closely during pregnancy, through delivery, and in the immediate postpartum period [N6-F4]. It also emphasizes that the risk of the fetus inheriting the bleeding tendency must be considered, and prenatal diagnosis may be performed with chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis [N6-F4]. This means that differential diagnosis during pregnancy must include not only the immediate bleeding disorder but also the possibility of a hereditary condition affecting the fetus. The pregnancy-specific management guidance further notes that maternal bleeding complications may require blood transfusion, and that specialized care involving hematologists, obstetricians, and anesthesiologists is essential [N6-F4]. Therefore, the diagnostic process must balance maternal bleeding risk with fetal safety and ensure that prenatal diagnosis and counseling are part of the care plan [N6-F4][N6-R1].

### 12) Integrated practical takeaways
In practice, identifying type 1 and type 2 VWD during pregnancy should follow this integrated approach:
- **Start with clinical suspicion** and a careful bleeding history [N1-F1][N4-R4];
- **Use screening tests** of VWF:Ag, FVIII:C, and VWF activity [N2-R2][N2-R3];
- **Use type-specific assays** such as ristocetin cofactor when the subtype is unclear [N2-R5];
- **Interpret results in pregnancy context**, recognizing that VWF and FVIII can rise substantially and platelet-function tests are not reliable [N5-F3][N7-R1][N7-R2];
- **Be aware that pregnancy can mask type 2 disease**, especially when VWF:RCo/VWF:Ag ratios are abnormal [N5-F3];
- **Distinguish inherited from acquired bleeding disorders** and consider thrombocytopenia and other acquired conditions [N3-R2][N3-R4][N6-R3];
- **Balance maternal bleeding risk with fetal safety**, including prenatal diagnosis and multidisciplinary management [N6-F4][N6-R1].

### 13) Bottom line
Overall, the recommended diagnostic steps for VWD are clear and evidence-based, but pregnancy introduces major challenges. Routine tests may be normal or falsely elevated, platelet-function tests are not specific, and the distinction between inherited and acquired disease is often difficult. Type 1 and type 2 VWD differ mainly by qualitative versus quantitative defect, and pregnancy can mask type 2 disease while potentially normalizing type 1 testing. The correct management plan depends on accurate diagnosis, careful interpretation of pregnancy-related changes, and subtype-specific care [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5][N4-F2][N5-F3][N6-F4].
